source_text: Potestas uero dupliciter aduersum nos datur, uel ad poenam cum delinquimus uel ad gloriam cum probamur: sicuti de Iob factum uidemus manifestante Deo et dicente: ecce omnia quaecumque habet in tuas manus do: sed ipsum caue ne tangas. et Dominus in euangelio loquitur tempore passionis: nullam haberes potestatem aduersum me nisi data esset tibi desuper. quando autem rogamus ne in temptationem ueniamus, admonemur infirmitatis et inbecillitatis nostrae dum sic rogamus, ne quis se insolenter extollat, ne quis sibi superbe adque adroganter aliquid adsumat, ne quis aut confessionis aut passionis gloriam suam ducat, cum Dominus ipse humilitatem docens dixerit: uigilate et orate, ne ueniatis in temptationem: spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma, ut dum praecedit humilis et summissa confessio et datur totum Deo quidquid suppliciter cum timore et honore Dei petitur ipsius pietate praestetur.
thought_title: Power given for punishment or for glory
orientation: Cyprian is explaining the petition 'lead us not into temptation' by showing that power over us is given by God either to punish sin or to prove the righteous, and that the petition teaches humility.
pass_a_gloss: But power is given against us in two ways, either for punishment when we sin or for glory when we are tested: just as we see it was done concerning Job, with God declaring and saying: behold, all things whatever he has I give into your hands: but beware that you do not touch him. And the Lord in the Gospel speaks at the time of his passion: you would have no power against me unless it had been given to you from above. But when we ask that we not come into temptation, we are reminded of our weakness and feebleness while we ask in this way, so that no one may insolently exalt himself, so that no one may proudly and arrogantly claim anything for himself, so that no one may consider the glory of confession or of suffering to be his own, since the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: watch and pray, so that you do not come into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak, so that while a humble and submissive confession goes before and everything is given to God, whatever is asked suppliantly with fear and honor of God may be granted by his own mercy.

choices.english: for glory when we are tested
choices.why: Keeps the passive sense of probamur and the contrast with punishment; 'tested' preserves the idea of God proving the righteous.
rejected: for glory when we are tried
for glory when we are proved

choices.why: Renders the ablative absolute literally and keeps the two participles distinct.

choices.english: so that no one may insolently exalt himself
choices.why: Preserves the reflexive se and the subjunctive force of the purpose clause.
rejected: that no one should exalt himself

choices.term: confessionis aut passionis gloriam suam ducat
choices.english: may consider the glory of confession or of suffering to be his own
choices.why: Ducat with double accusative is rendered as 'consider...to be his own' to keep the claim of ownership explicit.
rejected: may claim the glory of confession or passion as his own
may take the glory of confession or suffering for himself

choices.term: spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma
choices.english: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak
choices.why: Standard literal rendering of the gospel citation, keeping quidem...autem as indeed...but.
rejected: the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak
the spirit is ready but the flesh is weak

choices.english: may be granted by his own mercy
choices.why: Pietas here means God's merciful goodness; 'mercy' fits the context of humble petition better than 'piety'.
rejected: may be granted by his piety
may be bestowed by his goodness

pass_b_english: Power is given against us in two ways: either for punishment when we sin, or for glory when we are tested. We see this in what happened to Job, with God declaring and saying: Look, I give into your hands everything he has; only beware not to touch him (Job 1:12). And the Lord says in the Gospel at the time of his passion: You would have no power against me unless it had been given to you from above (John 19:11). When we ask not to come into temptation, we are reminded of our weakness and feebleness by the very prayer we make, so that no one may insolently exalt himself, no one may arrogantly and proudly claim anything for himself, no one may consider the glory of confession or of suffering to be his own. For the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: Watch and pray, so that you do not come into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41). In this way, when a humble and lowly confession goes before, and everything asked in supplication with fear and honor of God is given wholly to God, it may be granted by his own mercy.
